extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students of American government and foreign policy; general readers studying U.S. institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory textbook guidance on (a) the role and political implications of federal judicial review and (b) the institutions, ranks, duties, privileges, and desired qualifications for U.S. diplomatic and consular representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for declaring a law void
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court 'will not declare a law void except when there is no doubt in the mind of the Court as to its unconstitutionality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement of judicial restraint: the Court should avoid declaring statutes unconstitutional unless there is no doubt. Context notes that the Supreme Court nonetheless declared more than 200 state statutes invalid in the period under discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal judicial review over state acts
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of the Court to pass upon the acts of state governments (judicial review) is grounded in the same logic as Marshall's opinion in Marbury v. Madison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains rationale: without a final tribunal to give uniformity, conflicting state-court decisions would cause endless complications; Jeffersonian objections existed but no adequate plan was offered to resolve federal-state disputes without a national judicial arbiter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition that judicial decisions are political in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost every important statute is a political act, and the power to declare such an act null and void is a political power, though exercised as a judicial decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: Supreme Court decisions often draw the Court into partisan controversies (examples: Dred Scott, the income-tax decision). Political criticism of the Court is to be expected when judicial rulings affect fundamental party interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: President as official spokesman in foreign affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution implicitly makes the President the official spokesman of the nation in foreign matters by giving him the power to appoint representatives abroad and to negotiate treaties with Senate approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The President is the sole official agent through whom foreign ministers can communicate with the United States; this centralizes external communications and representation in the executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of State conducts the actual work of foreign affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: While the President is the official spokesman, the actual conduct of foreign affairs is vested in the Secretary of State, who performs duties intrusted by the President relative to correspondences, commissions, instructions, and negotiations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department of State is the legal organ of communication between the President and foreign countries; the Secretary manages business as the President directs and handles important policy matters personally or with the Cabinet.

rubrics_metrics.name: All official communications to foreign governments must run through the Department of State
rubrics_metrics.description: No officer of the United States, civil or military, should address a foreign government except through the Department of State or our diplomatic representatives abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even Presidential autograph letters are countersigned and transmitted by the Secretary of State so communications appear officially through that agency. Historical practice and Department routine enforce this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and reciprocal rank of diplomatic representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Diplomatic representatives are classified (1) ambassadors extraordinary and plenipotentiary; (2) envoys extraordinary and ministers plenipotentiary and special commissioners; (3) ministers resident; (4) charges d'affaires; and Congress (1893) provided that a U.S. representative should have the same rank as the representative of that country to the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: the U.S. returns equivalent rank when other nations send ambassadors, entailing higher costs; ranks derive from European court ceremonials and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination and Senate appointment requirement for diplomats
rubrics_metrics.description: All diplomatic representatives are nominated by the President and appointed by and with the advice and consent of the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional procedure is emphasized; surrounding text criticizes political patronage in appointments and points to reforms (examinations, promotions) to raise standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointments should be based on qualifications, not political spoils
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the diplomatic and consular services require special knowledge and experience, representatives have too often been selected without regard to qualifications and as rewards for political service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform guidance: longer tenure, merit promotion from within the service, oral and written examinations to show fitness (Roosevelt orders, 1909 tougher exams, 1906 Consular Reorganization Act). Political patronage is identified as an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-nomination acceptability and formal induction of ministers
rubrics_metrics.description: In nominating ministers the President should ascertain whether a proposed appointee is personally acceptable to the government to which he is to be sent; after appointment, a minister receives a formal letter of credence and on arrival enters communication with the foreign government's foreign affairs representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customary induction practices: predecessor remains until the new minister's arrival and arranges induction; ceremonials and audience with the head of government follow the customs of the host country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diplomatic privileges and immunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Under international law a diplomatic representative's residence is protected, he is entitled to special protection while travelling, and he and his official family (including domestic servants) are exempt from arrest — in short, from criminal and civil processes at all times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any injury or affront to a diplomat is an offence against the represented country; these privileges derive from rules of international comity and are central to the functioning of diplomacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily duties and unofficial/quiet nature of successful diplomacy
rubrics_metrics.description: A minister's duties are not confined to official communications; he should cultivate friendly personal relations with host-government officers and adapt to local modes so that he can obtain confidence and informal access to adjust matters as informally and genially as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success in diplomacy is often unheralded; informal and confidential interposition by ministers can avert imprisonment, loss of property, and public controversies. The report cited says a diplomat is successful in proportion to the tranquility he maintains in bilateral relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-interference in host-country politics and caution in public addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Diplomatic representatives of the United States should scrupulously abstain from interfering in the political controversies of the countries to which they are accredited, and ambassadors should avoid making public addresses on politics except with extreme caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern example: the House censured Mr. Bayard (1896) for a public speech criticizing the U.S. protective tariff; ambassadors making political remarks risk diplomatic censure and controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consuls as commercial agents with specific professional qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Consuls are primarily commercial agents who perform many routine duties; long experience, mastery of the local language, careful study of markets and export/import conditions, and some legal training are important qualifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically consular posts were political spoils; the 1906 Consular Reorganization Act sought to establish graded positions, merit promotion, and filling important vacancies by promotion or by appointment of candidates who passed oral and written exams. Rapid personnel turnover is an identified anti-pattern for effective consular work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consular grades and functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The consular service is divided into (1) consuls-general-at-large who inspect consulates worldwide; (2) consuls-general who supervise consular systems of particular countries; and (3) consuls stationed at innumerable points, with vice-consuls and consular agents under direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each grade has supervisory or local operational duties; organization and grading enable the extension of a merit system and more efficient commercial representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of special diplomatic missions for particular negotiations
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States employs special missions (special plenipotentiaries) for specific negotiations such as peace negotiations or opening relations (examples: 1898 commission to Paris to conclude treaty with Spain; Commodore Perry's special mission to Japan in 1852).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special missions are a recognized instrument for conducting important or exceptional foreign-policy tasks outside the routine diplomatic service.
